description: Japanese grammar points for the JP Verb Conjugation app. Hand-authored; run scripts/update_data.py after editing.

grammar.title: んです
grammar.summary: Marks a sentence as explanation, context or reason. Use んです after verbs and い-adjectives, and なんです after nouns and な-adjectives.

usages.heading: Asking for or giving a reason
usages.explanation: The most basic use. A question with んですか asks for the story behind something you can see or have just heard, and a statement with んです supplies it.

examples.jp: どうしたんですか。頭が痛いんです。
examples.en: What's wrong? I have a headache.

examples.jp: どうして遅れたんですか。電車が止まったんです。
examples.en: Why were you late? The train stopped.

usages.heading: Softening a request or a lead-in
usages.explanation: Before asking for something, んですが or んですけど sets the scene and leaves the request unsaid. It sounds much gentler than asking outright.

examples.jp: すみません、道を聞きたいんですが。
examples.en: Excuse me, I'd like to ask for directions.

examples.jp: ちょっと手伝ってほしいんですけど。
examples.en: I'd like a little help, if that's okay.

usages.heading: Refusing with a reason
usages.explanation: Turning a refusal into an explanation makes it softer and more polite than a flat no. Verbs in the potential form are very common here.

examples.jp: すみません、今日は行けないんです。
examples.en: Sorry, I can't go today.

examples.jp: お酒は飲めないんです。
examples.en: I can't drink alcohol.

usages.heading: Reacting to something you noticed
usages.explanation: With ね, んです shows you have just realized or been impressed by something.

examples.jp: 日本語が上手なんですね。
examples.en: Your Japanese is good, isn't it. I'm impressed.

examples.jp: 外は雨が降っているんですね。
examples.en: So it's raining outside.

usages.heading: Emphasis and background
usages.explanation: Use it to give the background to what you are about to say, to correct an assumption, or to put the focus on one part of the sentence.

examples.jp: 実は、まだ食べていないんです。
examples.en: Actually, I haven't eaten yet.

examples.jp: 昨日買ったのは、この本なんです。
examples.en: What I bought yesterday is this book.

usages.heading: Checking an inference
usages.explanation: You have guessed something from what you can see or hear, and you ask whether you are right.

examples.jp: 疲れているんですか。
examples.en: Are you tired? (You look it.)

examples.jp: 日本に住んでいたんですか。
examples.en: So you used to live in Japan?

usages.heading: Acknowledging what someone told you
usages.explanation: Saying そうなんですか shows you have taken in new information: "oh, is that so?" The casual version is そうなんだ.

examples.jp: 来月、京都に行くんです。そうなんですか。
examples.en: I'm going to Kyoto next month. Oh, really?

examples.jp: 来週、引っ越すんだ。そうなんだ。
examples.en: I'm moving next week. Oh, I see.

attachment.example: 食べるんです / 食べないんです / 食べたんです / 食べなかったんです
attachment.note: The polite form never comes before it: 食べますんです is wrong.

attachment.example: 高いんです / 高くないんです / 高かったんです / 高くなかったんです
静かなんです
attachment.note: The な is the plain だ turning into な before の, which is why it only appears here.

attachment.example: 学生なんです

attachment.pattern: stem + だった / じゃない + んです
attachment.example: 静かだったんです / 静かじゃないんです

attachment.pattern: noun + だった / じゃない + んです
attachment.example: 学生だったんです / 学生じゃないんです

conjugations.note: Asks for an explanation.

conjugations.form: んですが / んですけど
conjugations.note: Sets the scene, often before a request.
Reacts to something you just noticed.
"Isn't it that...?" Used to suggest or double-check.
Denies the explanation. After a plain verb it can also mean "don't do it!" (see Watch out).
Rare. The past normally goes on the verb instead: 食べたんです.
Adds "you know" when telling someone.
A casual question. の？ is very common and neutral.
As a statement (行くの。) it sounds softer and, for many speakers, feminine.
The written or formal version of んです.

pitfalls.heading: Negating it is not a plain refusal
pitfalls.explanation: 食べないんです explains why you are not eating. But 食べるんじゃない (or 食べるんじゃありません) is a strong "don't eat!", and 食べたんじゃない means "it's not that I ate".

examples.jp: 今は食べないんです。
examples.en: I'm not eating right now (and there's a reason).

examples.jp: そんなに食べるんじゃない。
examples.en: Don't eat so much!

examples.jp: 食べたんじゃないんです。
examples.en: It's not that I ate it.

pitfalls.heading: Don't overuse it
pitfalls.explanation: For plain new information, use the ordinary polite form. Adding んです makes a sentence sound like an explanation. And んですか asks for one, so it can sound probing or, in the wrong tone, demanding or aggressive. It is not a neutral question marker.

examples.jp: 毎日学校に行きます。
examples.en: I go to school every day. (a plain statement)

examples.jp: 毎日学校に行くんです。
examples.en: I go to school every day. (explaining, e.g. why you get up early)

pitfalls.heading: The past goes on the verb
pitfalls.explanation: To explain something that happened, put the past tense on the verb before んです. 〜んでした exists but is rare.

examples.jp: 昨日は早く寝たんです。
examples.en: I went to bed early yesterday.

grammar.title: 可能形
grammar.summary: The potential form says that someone can do something, or that the situation allows it: 食べられる, 飲める, できる. It conjugates as a ru-verb.

usages.heading: Ability
usages.explanation: The person has the skill or knowledge to do it. The thing they can do usually takes が.

examples.jp: 私は漢字が読めます。
examples.en: I can read kanji.

examples.jp: 兄は三キロ泳げます。
examples.en: My older brother can swim three kilometres.

usages.heading: Possibility and circumstances
usages.explanation: This is not about skill: the situation allows it, or doesn't. The negative is the polite way to decline, and with んです it becomes an explanation (see the んです lesson).

examples.jp: 今日は行けません。
examples.en: I can't go today.

examples.jp: この店ではカードが使えます。
examples.en: You can use cards at this shop.

examples.jp: 明日なら会えます。
examples.en: I can meet you tomorrow.

usages.heading: が, を and には
usages.explanation: The thing that can be done normally takes が. を is very common in speech and is fine too. The person who can (or can't) often takes には, especially when contrasting with other people.

examples.jp: すしが食べられますか。
examples.en: Can you eat sushi? (the standard particle)

examples.jp: すしを食べられますか。
examples.en: Can you eat sushi? (common in speech)

examples.jp: 私にはこの漢字が読めません。
examples.en: I can't read this kanji. (for me, at least)

usages.heading: できる and ことができる
usages.explanation: できる is the potential of する, and works as a verb of its own: a noun + ができる means being able to do it, or being good at it. ことができる is a more formal way to say "can" that works with any verb, and is common in writing and speeches.

examples.jp: 日本語ができますか。
examples.en: Do you speak Japanese?

examples.jp: 泳ぐことができます。
examples.en: I can swim. (formal)

examples.jp: あしたは勉強できません。
examples.en: I can't study tomorrow.

usages.heading: 見える / 聞こえる vs 見られる / 聞ける
usages.explanation: 見える and 聞こえる are verbs of their own: something is visible or audible without you trying. 見られる and 聞ける are the potential forms: you have the chance or the ability to watch or listen.

examples.jp: 富士山が見えます。
examples.en: Mt. Fuji is visible from here.

examples.jp: 鳥の声が聞こえます。
examples.en: I can hear birds singing.

examples.jp: この曲は無料で聞けます。
examples.en: You can listen to this song for free.

attachment.example: 食べる → 食べられる / 見る → 見られる
attachment.note: For ru-verbs this is identical to the passive form. Context tells them apart (see Watch out).

attachment.pattern: change the last kana to its え-sound, then る
attachment.example: 飲む → 飲める / 書く → 書ける / 話す → 話せる / 買う → 買える / 泳ぐ → 泳げる / 待つ → 待てる / 死ぬ → 死ねる / 遊ぶ → 遊べる / 取る → 取れる
attachment.note: The endings move like this: う→え, く→け, ぐ→げ, す→せ, つ→て, ぬ→ね, ぶ→べ, む→め, る→れ.

attachment.example: 勉強する → 勉強できる
attachment.note: できる is a different verb, not する with an ending added.

attachment.example: 来る → 来られる
attachment.note: Written 来られる and read こられる. It looks like the passive too.

conjugations.note: Polite present. A potential verb is itself a ru-verb, so it conjugates like one: drop る and add the ending. For u-verbs the ending follows the え-sound: 飲めます, 書けます, 話せます.
U-verbs: 飲めません.
U-verbs: 飲めました.
U-verbs: 飲めませんでした.
The plain form, which is the potential form itself. U-verbs: 飲める, 書ける, 話せる.
U-verbs: 飲めない.
U-verbs: 飲めた.
U-verbs: 飲めなかった.
The て-form: for linking clauses and giving reasons, as in 会えてうれしいです. It is not used for requests (食べられてください is wrong). U-verbs: 飲めて.
Dictionary form + ことができる. Works with any verb. Stiffer, and common in writing.

pitfalls.heading: Potential looks like the passive
pitfalls.explanation: For ru-verbs and 来る the two forms are spelled the same, so only context tells them apart. U-verbs differ: 飲める is potential and 飲まれる is passive.

examples.jp: 私は納豆が食べられます。
examples.en: I can eat natto. (potential)

examples.jp: ケーキを妹に食べられた。
examples.en: My little sister ate my cake. (passive: the cake "got eaten", and I'm not happy about it)

pitfalls.heading: ら抜き言葉 (colloquial contraction)
pitfalls.explanation: Many speakers drop the ら: 食べれる, 起きれる, 来れる. It is very common in speech and is treated as casual or non-standard in writing and exams. It only happens with ru-verbs and 来る; u-verbs never had a ら to drop.

examples.jp: 朝は早く起きれない。
examples.en: I can't get up early. (colloquial)

examples.jp: 朝は早く起きられない。
examples.en: I can't get up early. (standard)

pitfalls.heading: "Can" is not "may"
pitfalls.explanation: The potential says that something is possible or within your ability. To ask for or give permission, use 〜てもいいです instead.

examples.jp: ここでは写真が撮れます。
examples.en: You can take photos here. (it's possible)

examples.jp: ここで写真を撮ってもいいです。
examples.en: You may take photos here. (permission)

pitfalls.heading: Verbs with no potential
pitfalls.explanation: ある has no potential form. ありえる is a separate word meaning "can happen"; it does not mean "can have". わかる already means "can be understood", so it needs none. That is why the app shows no potential section for ある.

examples.jp: そんなことはありえない。
examples.en: That can't happen.

grammar.title: はず・かもしれない・わけ
grammar.summary: Three ways to say how things stand: はず (I expect so, because it makes sense), かもしれない (maybe), and わけ (that is how it works out). All three come after a plain form.

usages.heading: はず: what you expect
usages.explanation: はず says that, going by what you know, something should be the case. It is a judgement from reasons, not a hunch, so it is stronger than かもしれない.

examples.jp: 田中さんはもう家に着いたはずです。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka should have arrived home by now.

examples.jp: この道を行けば、駅に出るはずだ。
examples.en: If you go this way, you should come out at the station.

usages.heading: はず: what was supposed to happen
usages.explanation: はずだった says that something was expected or planned and did not turn out that way. はずがない (or はずはない) says there is no way it can be true.

examples.jp: 会議は三時からのはずでしたが、まだ始まっていません。
examples.en: The meeting was supposed to start at three, but it hasn't started yet.

examples.jp: あの人が知らないはずがない。
examples.en: There's no way that person doesn't know.

usages.heading: かもしれない: maybe
usages.explanation: かもしれない says that something is possible, with no claim about how likely. Polite speech uses かもしれません, and in casual speech it often shrinks to かも.

examples.jp: 明日は雨が降るかもしれない。
examples.en: It might rain tomorrow.

examples.jp: 山田さんは来ないかもしれません。
examples.en: Mr. Yamada may not come.

examples.jp: これ、ちょっと高いかも。
examples.en: This might be a bit expensive.

usages.heading: わけ: that is how it works out
usages.explanation: わけ (訳) means a reason or a line of reasoning. 〜わけだ says that something follows naturally from what you already know, like "no wonder" or "so that's why".

examples.jp: 毎日練習しているから、上手なわけだ。
examples.en: He practises every day, so no wonder he's good.

examples.jp: なるほど、だから眠いわけですね。
examples.en: I see, so that's why you're sleepy.

usages.heading: わけがない and わけではない
usages.explanation: わけがない says that something cannot be so. わけではない does not deny the whole sentence but one conclusion that someone might draw, and so it means "it's not that...".

examples.jp: そんなに早く終わるわけがない。
examples.en: There's no way it'll be over that quickly.

examples.jp: 嫌いなわけではありません。ただ、時間がないんです。
examples.en: It's not that I dislike it. I just don't have the time.

examples.jp: お酒が飲めないわけじゃないよ。
examples.en: It's not that I can't drink.

usages.heading: How sure are you?
usages.explanation: In order of confidence: かもしれない is a possibility, はず is an expectation backed by reasons, and 〜に違いない is close to certain. わけ is different: it does not guess at all but shows that a result follows from what you know.

examples.jp: 雨が降るかもしれない。
examples.en: It might rain. (possible)

examples.jp: 雨が降るはずだ。天気予報でそう言っていた。
examples.en: It should rain. The forecast said so. (expected)

attachment.pattern: plain form + はず / かもしれない / わけ
attachment.example: 行くはず / 行かないはず / 行ったはず / 行かなかったはず
attachment.note: The same plain forms (present and past, positive and negative) come before all three. The polite ます form never does.

attachment.pattern: plain form + はず / かもしれない / わけ
attachment.example: 高いはず / 高くないはず / 高かったはず

attachment.pattern: stem + な + はず / わけ; stem + かもしれない
attachment.example: 静かなはず / 静かなわけ / 静かかもしれない
attachment.note: かもしれない takes the bare stem. はず and わけ take な, as before any noun.

attachment.pattern: noun + の + はず; noun + かもしれない; noun + な + わけ
attachment.example: 学生のはず / 学生かもしれない / 学生なわけがない
attachment.note: かもしれない takes the bare noun. In the present, だ is dropped: 学生だかもしれない is wrong.

conjugations.note: Polite present. 〜はずでした for the past ("was supposed to").
"There is no way." 〜はずはありません is the same.
Polite maybe.
"It follows that..."
"It's not that..."
Plain present. 〜はずだった for the past.
Often shortened to かも, or かもね when talking with a friend.
"No way."
The spoken form of わけではない.

pitfalls.heading: かもしれない takes no だ
pitfalls.explanation: Before かもしれない, a noun or na-adjective stays bare. 学生だかもしれない and 静かだかもしれない are wrong; say 学生かもしれない and 静かかもしれない.

examples.jp: あの人は先生かもしれません。
examples.en: That person might be a teacher.

pitfalls.heading: わけ and んです both explain, in different ways
pitfalls.explanation: んです offers or asks for a reason for a situation in front of you. わけだ concludes from what you already know that the result is only natural. And わけではない denies only one conclusion that someone might draw: "it's not that...".

examples.jp: 遅れたのは、電車が止まったからなんです。
examples.en: I was late because the train stopped. (giving a reason)

examples.jp: 電車が止まったから、遅れたわけだ。
examples.en: The train stopped, so that's why they were late. (drawing a conclusion)

pitfalls.heading: わけにはいかない
pitfalls.explanation: This is a fixed phrase meaning "I cannot, for some reason", often a duty or a social rule. 行かないわけにはいかない means "I can't not go", that is, "I have to go".

examples.jp: 明日は大事な会議だから、休むわけにはいかない。
examples.en: Tomorrow is an important meeting, so I can't take the day off.

examples.jp: 友達の結婚式だから、行かないわけにはいかない。
examples.en: It's a friend's wedding, so I can't not go.

grammar.title: べき・ものだ
grammar.summary: べき says what someone should do, as advice or a moral judgement. ものだ states how things are in general, or remembers how things used to be.

usages.heading: べき: what someone should do
usages.explanation: Put べき after the dictionary form of a verb, then だ or です. It is a judgement about right and wrong, so it can sound strong.

examples.jp: もっと野菜を食べるべきだ。
examples.en: You should eat more vegetables.

examples.jp: 約束は守るべきです。
examples.en: Promises should be kept.

usages.heading: べきではない: what someone should not do
usages.explanation: べきではない (or べきじゃない in speech) says that something should not be done.

examples.jp: ここで大きな声を出すべきではありません。
examples.en: You shouldn't raise your voice here.

examples.jp: 人の悪口を言うべきじゃない。
examples.en: You shouldn't speak ill of others.

usages.heading: べきだった: should have
usages.explanation: In the past, べきだった says that something should have been done and wasn't. It carries regret or blame.

examples.jp: もっと早く言うべきだった。
examples.en: I should have said so sooner.

examples.jp: 昨日、休むべきでした。
examples.en: I should have rested yesterday.

usages.heading: ものだ: how things are
usages.explanation: ものだ presents something as a general truth or as human nature. The sentence is about people or things in general, not about one case.

examples.jp: 人は誰でも間違えるものです。
examples.en: Everyone makes mistakes.

examples.jp: 子供は遊ぶものだ。
examples.en: Children play. (that's what they do)

usages.heading: ものだ: remembering
usages.explanation: With the past plain form and a word like よく, ものだ looks back on something that used to happen again and again.

examples.jp: 子供のころ、よくこの川で泳いだものだ。
examples.en: When I was little, I used to swim in this river all the time.

examples.jp: 学生のころは、毎日友達と遊んだものです。
examples.en: When I was a student, I would play with my friends every day.

usages.heading: ものだ: feeling
usages.explanation: After an adjective, ものだ turns the sentence into an exclamation, often with ね.

examples.jp: 時間がたつのは早いものですね。
examples.en: Time really does fly, doesn't it.

examples.jp: 人の気持ちとは不思議なものだ。
examples.en: How strange people's feelings are.

usages.heading: ものではない: it isn't done
usages.explanation: ものではない after a verb says that something is not the done thing. It is common when scolding or advising.

examples.jp: 人の悪口を言うものではありません。
examples.en: One shouldn't speak ill of others.

examples.jp: 夜遅くに電話をかけるものではない。
examples.en: You shouldn't phone people late at night.

attachment.example: 食べるべき / 行くべき / 守るべき
attachment.note: する has two forms: するべき and すべき, which mean the same. The negative uses べきではない and does not change the verb: 食べるべきではない.

attachment.example: 忘れるものだ / 忘れたものだ
attachment.note: The present form states a general truth. The past た-form recalls how things used to be.

attachment.example: 早いものだ / 難しいものだ
attachment.note: Used as an exclamation.

attachment.example: 不思議なものだ / 大変なものだ

conjugations.note: "Should." 〜べきでした is "should have".
"Should not."
Polite ものだ. 〜ものでした for memories.
"It isn't done."
Plain "should". 〜べきだった is "should have".
The spoken form of べきではない.
Also 〜ものじゃない in speech.

pitfalls.heading: べき can sound bossy
pitfalls.explanation: べき is a judgement, and it is not a gentle suggestion. For gentler advice, use ほうがいい instead (see below), or turn the advice into a question.

examples.jp: もっと寝たほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: You should get more sleep. (softer than 寝るべきです)

pitfalls.heading: べき needs the dictionary form
pitfalls.explanation: The ます form and the past form do not come before べき. To say "should have", move the tense onto だ: 行くべきだった, not 行ったべき.

examples.jp: もっと勉強するべきだった。
examples.en: I should have studied more.

pitfalls.heading: ものだ is not the same as もの
pitfalls.explanation: もの on its own is a noun for a thing. ものだ is a fixed ending that turns the sentence into a statement of how things are or were, so it never refers to a particular object.

examples.jp: これは父にもらったものです。
examples.en: This is something I got from my father. (a thing)

examples.jp: 本は面白いものだ。
examples.en: Books are interesting, as a rule. (a general truth)

grammar.title: よう・みたい・そう・らしい
grammar.summary: Four ways to talk about what you see, hear or infer: ようだ and みたいだ (it seems, like), そうだ (it looks like, or I hear), and らしい (apparently, or typical of).

usages.heading: ようだ and みたいだ: it seems
usages.explanation: Use ようだ when you judge from what you can see, hear or feel yourself. みたいだ means the same and is more casual.

examples.jp: 誰かいるようです。
examples.en: It seems someone is there.

examples.jp: 外は寒いみたいだ。
examples.en: It seems cold outside.

usages.heading: Like something else
usages.explanation: The same words also mean "like". The adverb is ように, and before a noun it is ような or みたいな.

examples.jp: あの人は子供のように笑う。
examples.en: He laughs like a child.

examples.jp: 夢みたいな話ですね。
examples.en: It sounds like a dream.

usages.heading: そう: it looks like
usages.explanation: After a stem, そう says how something looks or that it is about to happen. It is your impression, and not something you were told.

examples.jp: このケーキはおいしそうです。
examples.en: This cake looks delicious.

examples.jp: 今にも雨が降りそうだ。
examples.en: It looks like it's going to rain at any moment.

usages.heading: そう: I hear
usages.explanation: After a plain form, そうだ passes on something you heard. It is hearsay and does not mean you can see it yourself.

examples.jp: 明日は雨が降るそうです。
examples.en: I hear it's going to rain tomorrow.

examples.jp: 田中さんは来ないそうだ。
examples.en: I hear Mr. Tanaka isn't coming.

usages.heading: らしい: apparently
usages.explanation: らしい also reports what you have heard or worked out, and often implies some evidence. It is less direct than ようだ.

examples.jp: 山田さんは風邪をひいたらしい。
examples.en: Apparently Mr. Yamada caught a cold.

examples.jp: 駅の前に新しい店ができるらしいです。
examples.en: I hear a new shop is opening in front of the station.

usages.heading: らしい: typical of
usages.explanation: After a noun, らしい can instead describe what is typical of it. It is a compliment: it fits what it should be.

examples.jp: 今日は春らしい天気ですね。
examples.en: It's spring-like weather today.

examples.jp: 学生らしい服を着なさい。
examples.en: Wear clothes that suit a student.

attachment.pattern: plain form + ようだ / みたいだ / らしい / そうだ (hearsay)
attachment.example: 行くようだ / 行ったみたいだ / 行かないらしい / 行くそうだ
attachment.note: These four all take the plain form. The polite ます form never comes before them.

attachment.example: 食べ + そうだ → 食べそうだ / 降り + そうだ → 降りそうだ
attachment.note: This is the "it looks like" そう. Compare 食べるそうだ (I hear he eats).

attachment.pattern: plain form + ようだ / みたいだ / らしい / そうだ (hearsay)
attachment.example: 高いようだ / 高いみたいだ / 高いらしい / 高いそうだ
おいしい → おいしそう / 高い → 高そう
attachment.note: いい becomes よさそう and ない becomes なさそう.

attachment.pattern: stem + な + よう; stem + みたい; stem + らしい; stem + だそうだ
attachment.example: 静かなようだ / 静かみたいだ / 静からしい / 静かだそうだ
attachment.note: ようだ takes な, みたいだ and らしい take the bare stem, and the hearsay そうだ keeps だ.

attachment.example: 元気 → 元気そう / 好き → 好きそう
attachment.note: "Looks like".

attachment.pattern: noun + の + よう; noun + みたい; noun + らしい; noun + だそうだ
attachment.example: 子供のようだ / 子供みたいだ / 子供らしい / 子供だそうだ
attachment.note: ようだ takes の, みたいだ and らしい take the bare noun, and the hearsay そうだ keeps だ. 子供らしい can also mean "childlike".

conjugations.note: Before a noun: 〜ような. As an adverb: 〜ように.
Looks like, or I hear. Before a noun, the "looks like" one is 〜そうな: おいしそうなケーキ.
Apparently.
Before a noun: 〜みたいな. As an adverb: 〜みたいに.
Looks like, or I hear.
Apparently. 〜らしくない means "not like X" or "unbecoming of X": 彼らしくない.

pitfalls.heading: Two meanings of そう
pitfalls.explanation: The same two syllables mean different things depending on what they attach to. On a stem they describe how it looks to you, and on a plain form they report hearsay.

examples.jp: あの店のラーメンはおいしそうです。
examples.en: That shop's ramen looks delicious. (you can see it)

examples.jp: あの店のラーメンはおいしいそうです。
examples.en: I hear that shop's ramen is delicious. (somebody told you)

pitfalls.heading: いい and ない before そう
pitfalls.explanation: With そう ("looks like"), いい becomes よさそう and ない becomes なさそう, and neither is attached as it is. This is a very common mistake.

examples.jp: 今日は天気がよさそうです。
examples.en: The weather looks good today.

examples.jp: 時間がなさそうですね。
examples.en: You don't look like you have time.

pitfalls.heading: ようだ and らしい are not the same
pitfalls.explanation: ようだ or みたいだ is your own impression, from something you have observed. らしい is for something you have heard or worked out from signs, and so you did not see it yourself.

examples.jp: 窓が開いているようだ。
examples.en: The window seems to be open. (your own impression, for example you feel a draft)

examples.jp: 窓が開いているらしい。
examples.en: Apparently the window is open. (you were told)

grammar.title: っぽい
grammar.summary: っぽい adds the feel of something: -ish, like, or prone to. It attaches to nouns, verb stems and い-adjective stems, and the result is an い-adjective.

usages.heading: -ish: it has the look or feel of
usages.explanation: After a noun, っぽい says that something is like it or looks like it. After a colour, it means a bit of that colour.

examples.jp: このスープは水っぽい。
examples.en: This soup is watery.

examples.jp: 黒っぽい服を着ています。
examples.en: I'm wearing blackish clothes.

examples.jp: 今日はちょっと熱っぽいです。
examples.en: I feel a bit feverish today.

usages.heading: Prone to
usages.explanation: After the ます stem of a verb, っぽい says that someone does something easily or often. It is mostly used with a handful of verbs.

examples.jp: 父は忘れっぽいです。
examples.en: My father is forgetful.

examples.jp: 弟は飽きっぽい。
examples.en: My little brother gets bored easily.

usages.heading: Slightly, and not in a good way
usages.explanation: After an い-adjective stem, っぽい often gives a slightly negative impression, such as cheap-looking.

examples.jp: この時計は安っぽく見える。
examples.en: This watch looks cheap.

examples.jp: 安っぽいおもちゃを買ってしまった。
examples.en: I ended up buying a cheap-looking toy.

usages.heading: っぽい and らしい
usages.explanation: Both come after a noun. らしい is a compliment: it fits what it should be. っぽい only says that it looks like it, and is often a mild criticism.

examples.jp: 子供っぽい考えだ。
examples.en: That's a childish idea.

examples.jp: 子供らしい笑顔ですね。
examples.en: What a childlike smile.

attachment.example: 水っぽい / 子供っぽい / 白っぽい
attachment.note: Colours and states are common: 黒っぽい, 赤っぽい, 熱っぽい.

attachment.example: 忘れ + っぽい → 忘れっぽい / 飽き + っぽい → 飽きっぽい / 怒り + っぽい → 怒りっぽい
attachment.note: Only some verbs take it, so learn the common ones as vocabulary.

attachment.example: 安い → 安っぽい
attachment.note: Only a few adjectives take it.

conjugations.note: Polite present.
Negative. Also 〜っぽくありません.
It is an い-adjective, so it conjugates as one.
Negative.
Past.
て-form, for joining sentences.
Adverb: 子供っぽく話す.

pitfalls.heading: It is casual
pitfalls.explanation: っぽい belongs to spoken, everyday Japanese. Settled words such as 忘れっぽい, 安っぽい and 熱っぽい are fine in writing too, but a new one like 雨っぽい ("looks like rain") is casual.

examples.jp: 彼の話し方は少し子供っぽい。
examples.en: The way he talks is a little childish.

pitfalls.heading: It is an い-adjective
pitfalls.explanation: After you add っぽい, the whole word conjugates like any い-adjective: 子供っぽくない, 子供っぽかった, 子供っぽくて.

examples.jp: そのドレスはあまり安っぽくないですね。
examples.en: That dress doesn't look very cheap.

grammar.title: ている・てある
grammar.summary: ている describes an action in progress, or a state that results from an action: 食べている (is eating), 結婚している (is married). てある describes a state that someone left behind on purpose: 窓が開けてある.

usages.heading: In progress
usages.explanation: After a verb of an action that takes time, ている says that the action is going on now.

examples.jp: 今、ご飯を食べています。
examples.en: I'm eating a meal now.

examples.jp: 雨が降っています。
examples.en: It's raining.

usages.heading: A state that results
usages.explanation: After a verb that describes a change (結婚する, 知る, 持つ), ている does not mean that the change is happening. It describes the state you are in after it.

examples.jp: 田中さんは結婚しています。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka is married.

examples.jp: あの人を知っていますか。
examples.en: Do you know that person?

examples.jp: 私は車を持っています。
examples.en: I have a car.

usages.heading: Habits and ongoing situations
usages.explanation: ている also describes something you do regularly, or a situation that has been going on for some time.

examples.jp: 毎朝、走っています。
examples.en: I run every morning.

examples.jp: 兄は会社で働いています。
examples.en: My older brother works at a company.

examples.jp: 私は京都に住んでいます。
examples.en: I live in Kyoto.

usages.heading: てある: a state someone left
usages.explanation: てある says that someone did something on purpose and the result is still there. The thing that was affected is the subject, usually marked with が (or は), and the verb is one that takes an object.

examples.jp: 窓が開けてあります。
examples.en: The window has been opened. (someone did it, and it is still open)

examples.jp: 机の上にメモが置いてある。
examples.en: A note has been left on the desk.

examples.jp: ホテルはもう予約してあります。
examples.en: The hotel has already been booked.

usages.heading: ている or てある?
usages.explanation: ている describes a state without saying who caused it, and てある says that a person did it deliberately, often to be ready for something. Compare an intransitive verb with ている and a transitive verb with てある.

examples.jp: ドアが開いている。
examples.en: The door is open.

examples.jp: ドアが開けてある。
examples.en: The door has been left open. (someone did it on purpose)

attachment.example: 食べる → 食べている / 飲む → 飲んでいる / 書く → 書いている / 買う → 買っている / する → している / 来る → 来ている
attachment.note: The て-form comes from the verb as usual, and いる then conjugates like any ru-verb. In speech the い is often dropped: 食べてる. Verbs of existence and ability, such as ある and できる, are the exceptions.

attachment.example: 開ける → 開けてある / 書く → 書いてある / 置く → 置いてある / 予約する → 予約してある
attachment.note: Only verbs that take an object. An intransitive verb such as 開く uses ている instead: 開いている.

conjugations.note: Polite present. 〜ていました for the past, 〜ていません for the negative.
Negative. 〜ていませんでした for the past negative.
Plain present. Often shortened to 〜てる in speech.
Plain past.
Plain negative. 〜ていなかった for the past negative.
Polite. 〜てありません is the negative and 〜てありました the past.
Plain. Its negative is 〜てない, which is spelled like the spoken form of 〜ていない.

pitfalls.heading: 行っている and 来ている
pitfalls.explanation: With 行く and 来る, ている does not mean that the person is on the way. It describes the state after getting there: gone, or come.

examples.jp: 田中さんは今、大阪に行っています。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka has gone to Osaka. (and is there now)

examples.jp: 友達が来ています。
examples.en: My friend has come. (and is here)

pitfalls.heading: Knowing, and the negative
pitfalls.explanation: 知っている means "to know", but its negative is 知らない (or 知りません), and not 知っていない.

examples.jp: あの人のことは知りません。
examples.en: I don't know that person.

pitfalls.heading: てある needs a verb that takes an object
pitfalls.explanation: てある cannot follow a verb such as 開く or 始まる, because nobody does that to something. 窓が開けてある is right, and 窓が開いてある is not. To describe the state without a person behind it, use ている.

examples.jp: 窓が開けてあります。
examples.en: The window has been opened. (by someone)

grammar.title: てしまう・ておく
grammar.summary: てしまう says that something is completely done, or that it happened and you regret it. ておく says that you do something in advance, or leave something as it is.

usages.heading: てしまう: done completely
usages.explanation: After a verb, てしまう says that the action is finished, done and out of the way.

examples.jp: 宿題はもう全部やってしまいました。
examples.en: I've already finished all of my homework.

examples.jp: この本は昨日、全部読んでしまった。
examples.en: I finished the whole book yesterday.

usages.heading: てしまう: regret
usages.explanation: When something happened that you did not want, てしまう adds the feeling of "oh no" or "I'm sorry".

examples.jp: 財布を忘れてしまった。
examples.en: Oh no, I forgot my wallet.

examples.jp: 大事な書類をなくしてしまいました。
examples.en: Unfortunately, I lost an important document.

usages.heading: Casual ちゃう and じゃう
usages.explanation: In casual speech てしまう shrinks to ちゃう, and でしまう shrinks to じゃう. The past forms are ちゃった and じゃった.

examples.jp: あ、全部食べちゃった。
examples.en: Oops, I ate it all.

examples.jp: ジュースを飲んじゃった。
examples.en: I drank the juice. (and I shouldn't have)

usages.heading: ておく: getting ready
usages.explanation: ておく says that you do something now so that things are ready for later.

examples.jp: 旅行の前に、ホテルを予約しておきます。
examples.en: Before the trip, I'll book a hotel.

examples.jp: 友達が来る前に、部屋を掃除しておく。
examples.en: I'll clean the room before my friend comes.

usages.heading: ておく: leaving as it is
usages.explanation: ておく also says that you leave something in the state it is in. In requests it is very common, with ください.

examples.jp: 窓は開けておいてください。
examples.en: Please leave the window open.

examples.jp: 電気はつけておく。
examples.en: I'll leave the light on.

attachment.pattern: て-form + しまう / おく
attachment.example: 食べてしまう / 飲んでしまう / 書いてしまう / してしまう / 予約しておく / 書いておく
attachment.note: The same て-form as for ている. In casual speech: 食べちゃう, 飲んじゃう (しまう), and 書いとく, 読んどく (おく).

conjugations.note: Polite present. 〜てしまいました for the past.
Polite present. 〜ておきました for the past.
Plain. 〜てしまった for the past. The negative 〜てしまわない is rare, mostly in 〜てしまわないように.
Spoken form of 〜てしまう (〜じゃう after で). 〜ちゃった for the past.
Plain. 〜ておいた for the past, and 〜ておかない for the negative.
Spoken form of 〜ておく (〜どく after で).

pitfalls.heading: Completion or regret?
pitfalls.explanation: The same ending can mean either, and the situation tells you which. Finishing something you set out to do is completion, and something that simply happens to you is usually regret.

examples.jp: 宿題を全部やってしまったから、遊びに行ける。
examples.en: I've got all my homework done, so I can go out. (completion)

examples.jp: 夏休みが終わってしまった。
examples.en: The summer vacation is over, sadly. (regret)

pitfalls.heading: ておく or てある?
pitfalls.explanation: ておく is the action, done in advance by a person. てある is the state that it leaves. Both can describe the same hotel booking.

examples.jp: ホテルを予約しておきました。
examples.en: I booked the hotel in advance.

examples.jp: ホテルは予約してあります。
examples.en: The hotel is booked.

pitfalls.heading: ちゃう is casual
pitfalls.explanation: ちゃう, じゃう and とく are spoken forms. Use てしまう and ておく when writing, or when speaking politely.

examples.jp: 宿題を忘れてしまいました。
examples.en: I forgot my homework. (polite)

grammar.title: てみる・ながら
grammar.summary: てみる means "try doing it and see". ながら joins two actions that happen at the same time, and the second one is the main action.

usages.heading: てみる: try it and see
usages.explanation: てみる says that you do something to find out what it is like. The みる comes from 見る, but as a helper it is written in hiragana.

examples.jp: この料理を食べてみてください。
examples.en: Please try this dish.

examples.jp: このシャツを着てみてもいいですか。
examples.en: May I try this shirt on?

usages.heading: Trying, and wanting to try
usages.explanation: In the past, てみた says that you tried. てみたい says that you want to try.

examples.jp: 日本語で話してみました。
examples.en: I tried speaking in Japanese.

examples.jp: 新しいレストランに行ってみたいです。
examples.en: I want to try going to the new restaurant.

usages.heading: ながら: two things at once
usages.explanation: ながら joins two actions that one person does at the same time. The action before ながら is the background, and the action at the end is the main one.

examples.jp: 音楽を聞きながら、勉強します。
examples.en: I study while listening to music.

examples.jp: 歩きながら、電話をしています。
examples.en: I'm talking on the phone while walking.

usages.heading: Which action is the main one
usages.explanation: Swapping the two actions swaps what you are emphasizing, so choose the order by what you want to say.

examples.jp: テレビを見ながらご飯を食べる。
examples.en: I eat while watching television. (eating is the main thing)

examples.jp: ご飯を食べながらテレビを見る。
examples.en: I watch television while eating. (watching is the main thing)

attachment.example: 食べる → 食べてみる / 飲む → 飲んでみる / 書く → 書いてみる / する → してみる / 来る → 来てみる
attachment.note: みる then conjugates like any ru-verb: 食べてみます, 食べてみた, 食べてみない.

attachment.example: 食べる → 食べながら / 飲む → 飲みながら / 書く → 書きながら / する → しながら / 歌う → 歌いながら
attachment.note: The stem is the ます form without ます (食べ, 飲み, 書き, し, 歌い). ながら does not conjugate.

conjugations.note: Polite present. 〜てみました for the past.
"I want to try."
Plain. 〜てみた for the past, and 〜てみない for the negative.
"I want to try."
Does not change: it is used as it is in polite speech, and the tense and the politeness come from the main verb at the end.
The same in casual speech; the tense comes from the main verb at the end.

pitfalls.heading: ながら needs one person doing both
pitfalls.explanation: Both actions must be done by the same person, and both must be ongoing. For two people at the same time, use 間 (as in ている間): 私が料理をしている間、彼はテレビを見ていた. For one action after another, use the て-form.

examples.jp: 彼は歌いながら歩いている。
examples.en: He is walking while singing.

pitfalls.heading: The tense is on the last verb
pitfalls.explanation: ながら itself has no tense, so the whole sentence takes its tense from the final verb.

examples.jp: 昨日は音楽を聞きながら、勉強した。
examples.en: Yesterday I studied while listening to music.

pitfalls.heading: Written in hiragana
pitfalls.explanation: In this use, write みる in hiragana: 食べてみる, and not 食べて見る. 見る on its own means "to see", and the hiragana みる marks the helper.

examples.jp: もう一度、やってみます。
examples.en: I'll try it once more.

grammar.title: すぎる・やすい・にくい
grammar.summary: All three attach to the ます-stem, and すぎる also attaches to adjectives. すぎる means "too much", やすい means "easy to", and にくい means "hard to". The first becomes a ru-verb, and the other two become い-adjectives.

usages.heading: すぎる: too much
usages.explanation: After a verb stem, すぎる says that someone does something too much.

examples.jp: 昨日は食べすぎました。
examples.en: I ate too much yesterday.

examples.jp: 飲みすぎると、頭が痛くなります。
examples.en: If you drink too much, you get a headache.

usages.heading: すぎる after adjectives
usages.explanation: すぎる also follows an adjective, and then it means "too". An い-adjective drops the い, and a な-adjective drops な.

examples.jp: この本は難しすぎる。
examples.en: This book is too difficult.

examples.jp: この部屋は静かすぎて、落ち着かない。
examples.en: This room is too quiet, and I can't relax.

usages.heading: やすい: easy to, and apt to
usages.explanation: After a verb stem, やすい says that something is easy to do. It can also say that something tends to happen.

examples.jp: この靴は歩きやすいです。
examples.en: These shoes are easy to walk in.

examples.jp: 私は風邪をひきやすいです。
examples.en: I catch colds easily.

usages.heading: にくい: hard to
usages.explanation: After a verb stem, にくい says that something is hard to do.

examples.jp: この漢字は読みにくいです。
examples.en: This kanji is hard to read.

examples.jp: この箸は使いにくい。
examples.en: These chopsticks are hard to use.

usages.heading: Becoming easier or harder
usages.explanation: やすい and にくい are い-adjectives, so they conjugate like one: やすくなる, にくくない, やすかった.

examples.jp: ペンを変えたら、字が書きやすくなった。
examples.en: After I changed pens, writing got easier.

examples.jp: この道は歩きにくくなかった。
examples.en: This road wasn't hard to walk on.

attachment.pattern: ます-stem + すぎる / やすい / にくい
attachment.example: 食べる → 食べすぎる / 飲む → 飲みやすい / 読む → 読みにくい / する → しすぎる / 来る → きすぎる
attachment.note: The stem is the ます form without ます (食べ, 飲み, し, き).

attachment.example: 高い → 高すぎる / 難しい → 難しすぎる
attachment.note: いい becomes よすぎる. The negative ない (and 〜くない) becomes なさすぎる: 味がなさすぎる. Adjectives that merely end in ない are regular: 少ない → 少なすぎる, 危ない → 危なすぎる.

attachment.example: 静か → 静かすぎる / 元気 → 元気すぎる

conjugations.note: Polite present. 〜すぎました for the past. すぎる is a ru-verb.
"Easy to." 〜やすくないです for the negative.
"Hard to." 〜にくくないです for the negative.
Plain. 〜すぎた for the past, and 〜すぎない for the negative.
An い-adjective: 〜やすかった, 〜やすくない, 〜やすくて.
An い-adjective: 〜にくかった, 〜にくくない, 〜にくくて.

pitfalls.heading: いい and ない before すぎる
pitfalls.explanation: With すぎる, いい becomes よすぎる and ない becomes なさすぎる, and neither is attached as it is.

examples.jp: このスープは味がなさすぎる。
examples.en: This soup has far too little flavour.

examples.jp: この条件はよすぎる。
examples.en: These terms are too good. (too good to be true)

pitfalls.heading: すぎる is usually a complaint
pitfalls.explanation: The basic meaning is "too much", so even with a word that is normally good it is usually a complaint: この部屋はきれいすぎて落ち着かない. In casual speech it is also used as strong praise, as in このケーキ、おいしすぎる！

examples.jp: この部屋はきれいすぎて、落ち着かない。
examples.en: This room is so clean that I can't relax.

examples.jp: このケーキ、おいしすぎる！
examples.en: This cake is way too good! (praise)

pitfalls.heading: やすい is not 安い
pitfalls.explanation: The word for "cheap", 安い, sounds the same as やすい. After a verb stem it is the helper, which you write in hiragana: 書きやすい (easy to write), and not 書き安い.

examples.jp: この辞書は使いやすくて、安い。
examples.en: This dictionary is easy to use, and cheap.

grammar.title: 〜ので
grammar.summary: Gives a reason: "(reason), so (result)". Softer and more polite than から.

usages.heading: Reason, then result
usages.explanation: The reason comes first, then ので, then what follows from it. It sounds calm and considerate, so it suits explaining yourself or asking a favour.

examples.jp: 日本語はおもしろいので、勉強しています。
examples.en: Japanese is interesting, so I study it.

examples.jp: 日本人の友達がいるので、日本語を勉強しています。
examples.en: I have Japanese friends, so I study Japanese.

examples.jp: 雨なので、出かけません。
examples.en: It's raining, so I'm not going out.

attachment.example: 食べる → 食べるので / 食べた → 食べたので
高い → 高いので / 高くない → 高くないので

attachment.pattern: short form (だ → な) + ので
attachment.example: 静かだ → 静かなので / 静かだった → 静かだったので

attachment.pattern: short form (だ → な) + ので
attachment.example: 雨だ → 雨なので / 雨だった → 雨だったので

pitfalls.heading: な, not だ, before ので
pitfalls.explanation: In the present affirmative, な-adjectives and nouns take な before ので, never だ.

examples.jp: この部屋は静かなので、よく眠れます。
examples.en: This room is quiet, so I sleep well.

contrasts.explanation: Both give a reason. ので sounds softer and more polite, so it suits explaining yourself. から is more direct and can sound like an excuse or a demand.

examples.jp: 電車が遅れたので、遅刻しました。
examples.en: The train was late, so I was late. (polite explanation)

examples.jp: 電車が遅れたから、遅刻した。
examples.en: The train was late, that's why I was late. (blunt)

grammar.title: 〜ほうがいいです
grammar.summary: Advice: "you had better…" or "you had better not…".

usages.heading: Advice to do something
usages.explanation: Use the plain past (た-form) of the verb, even though the advice is about now or the future.

examples.jp: 早く寝たほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: You had better go to bed early.

usages.heading: Advice not to do something
usages.explanation: Use the plain negative (ない-form).

examples.jp: 今日は出かけないほうがいいです。
examples.en: You had better not go out today.

attachment.pattern: た-form + ほうがいいです
attachment.example: 寝る → 寝たほうがいいです

attachment.pattern: ない-form + ほうがいいです
attachment.example: 出かける → 出かけないほうがいいです

conjugations.note: Plain. Add よ to sound like friendly advice.

pitfalls.heading: Never なかったほうがいい
pitfalls.explanation: The negative stays in the present: 行かないほうがいい, not 行かなかったほうがいい.

contrasts.explanation: After the た-form the advice is pointed and personal. After the dictionary form it sounds like a general statement.

examples.jp: 薬を飲んだほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: You should take some medicine.

examples.jp: 毎日、水を飲むほうがいいです。
examples.en: Drinking water every day is better (in general).
